newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - U.K. oil industry gets double jobs boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.K. oil industry gets double jobs boost.

text.p: Britain's thriving oil and gas industry received a double boost on Tuesday when Anglo-Dutch giant Shell and Amerada Hess of the United States announced contracts which will secure nearly 3,000 jobs.

Shell said it was planning to award three seven-year contracts worth 650 million sterling ($1.08 billion) for engineering and maintenance services for its fields in the central and northern North Sea.

Brown and Root, a unit of Haliburton, which is expected to win one of the Shell contracts in partnership with Arabian Oil Co International (AOC), also picked up a $270 million contract to provide facilities for Hess' South Arne development in the Danish North Sea.
The Hess deal should guarantee the future of 900 jobs in the north of Scotland but the bigger prize will be the Shell Expro awards, made on behalf of Shell and its joint venture partner Exxon Corp.
"This represents an exciting development in the way in which we run our business," said Malcolm Brinded, Shell Expro's oil and technical services director.

"These contracts, which will help provide job security for about 2,00 skilled workers onshore and offshore, will initially be for a seven-year period, beginning next year, and potentially could be extended for the entire life of these facilities."

Engineering group AMEC, in line to win a chunk of Shell's business, said 600 jobs would be secured. Another potential beneficiary, John Wood Group, said about 800 of its employees would be safe, thanks to its $200 million slice of the cake.
"The primary benefit to us is the long-term stability of the work," said Derek Blackwood, managing director of Wood Group Engineering's integrated services business.
"If you have that sort of term of contract it allows you to do some long term planning," said a spokeswoman for the Brown and Root-AOC joint venture.

Industry executives said the new business would not only safeguard the future of several thousand employees but also held out the prospect of prolonging North Sea oil production, thanks to the related cost savings.

"We believe there is the potential for significantly improved effectiveness giving at least 15 percent savings in engineering and maintenance costs over the next few years, which will be vital to prolong field life in many cases to 2010 and beyond," said Brinded.

Britain's North Sea oil and gas industry is reliving the heady days of its first boom in the 1980s, employing over 300,000 people offshore and in related onshore services and contributing $3.6 billion to government coffers last year.

One of the secrets of its success has been an efficiency drive which has slashed production and development costs and a recent trend to encourage contractors to share in project risk in return for higher exposure to potential rewards and greater stability.

Shell's contracts, industry observers said, provided further evidence that contractors and oil companies had found a "win-win" formula which could ensure the competitiveness of the sector well into the next millenium.
Contractors gain the opportunity to offer their employees training and career development but face penalties if they fail to deliver on the terms of the award.
"Our profitability will be related to the savings we bring to the client," said Blackwood.
